title: Software development life cycle
examples: What is the difference between waterfall and agile?
Which method is better for a small project?
Can you explain the stages of the SDLC again?

explain.say: The software development life cycle is a process.
The waterfall model is a linear approach to development.
In waterfall, one stage must finish before the next starts.

draw.text: Waterfall: Finish one stage before next

explain.say: Agile is an iterative and incremental approach to building software.
A real-life example is building a small website for a club.
A common mistake is assuming waterfall is always better for all projects.

faq.q: What is the main difference between waterfall and agile?
faq.a: Waterfall is strictly sequential, while agile is cyclical and adaptive. It is important to remember that agile welcomes changes throughout the process. You could also ask: How do I compare these two methods? Or: Which method is more flexible?
asks: How do I compare these two methods?

faq.q: Does the SDLC always have the same stages?
faq.a: While the core stages are similar, the exact names and emphasis can change. The main stages usually involve planning, building, and testing. Another way to ask this is: Are the stages fixed? Or: What are the basic steps?

faq.q: When should I use the waterfall model?
faq.a: You should use waterfall when requirements are very clear and unlikely to change. This model works best when the scope is fixed from the start. You might ask: Is waterfall good for small projects? Or: When should I use a linear approach?
asks: Is waterfall good for small projects?
When should I use a linear approach?

faq.q: What does 'iterative' mean in the context of agile?
faq.a: Iterative means repeating a cycle of building and testing in small chunks. You build a little bit, test it, and then use that feedback to build the next little bit. Another way to ask is: Does agile repeat steps? Or: What is the repeating nature of agile?
asks: What is the repeating nature of agile?

faq.q: Is the maintenance stage part of the initial SDLC cycle?
faq.a: Yes, maintenance is often considered part of the full lifecycle, even after initial deployment. This stage involves fixing bugs or adding small improvements later on. You could also ask: Does the cycle end after launch? Or: What happens after deployment?
asks: Does the cycle end after launch?

facts: The SDLC provides a structured framework for software creation.
The waterfall model follows a strict, sequential progression.
Agile methodologies embrace change and work in short cycles called sprints.
Key stages include gathering requirements, designing, coding, testing, and deploying.

quiz.say: If a project's requirements are certain and unlikely to change, which model is generally suitable?
quiz.why: The waterfall model excels when requirements are stable because it demands upfront completion of each phase.

wrong.0: Choosing both is difficult; one methodology is usually preferred for a given project scope.
wrong.2: Agile is designed for changing requirements, making it less efficient if change is not expected.
wrong.3: The spiral model is more complex and usually reserved for very high-risk projects.

quiz.say: In the agile approach, what is the primary benefit of working in short cycles?
quiz.why: Short cycles allow developers to test working software frequently, catching errors early.

wrong.0: Agile prioritizes working software over exhaustive documentation.
wrong.1: Agile assumes change is possible, so zero risk is not guaranteed.
wrong.2: Planning is still necessary, but it is done in small increments.

quiz.say: A project where the customer frequently changes their mind about features should use a model that supports:
quiz.why: Flexibility and iteration are the core strengths of agile methodologies.

wrong.0: Strict sequence implies that changes are difficult or impossible to incorporate.
wrong.1: Relying only on upfront planning fails when requirements shift.
wrong.2: A single large phase cannot accommodate the constant adjustments needed.
